name: Computers
description: From Babbage's engines and room-sized machines to the PC, the laptop and the phone: the computers that mattered, generation by generation.

checkpoints.name: Before electronics
checkpoints.note: Charles Babbage designs mechanical calculating engines in the nineteenth century and Ada Lovelace writes about what such a machine could do. In 1936 Alan Turing describes a universal computing machine on paper.

checkpoints.name: First generation: vacuum tubes
checkpoints.note: Computers switch with vacuum tubes (valves). They fill a room, run hot and fail often, and each one is built by hand. Colossus, ENIAC, EDSAC and UNIVAC I belong here; the Z3, built from relays, is a step just before.

checkpoints.name: Second generation: transistors
checkpoints.note: The transistor replaces the tube: smaller, cooler, cheaper and far more reliable. Computers such as the IBM 1401 and 7090 move from laboratories into ordinary businesses, and languages like FORTRAN and COBOL arrive.

checkpoints.name: Third generation: integrated circuits
checkpoints.note: Many transistors are made together on one chip. IBM's System/360 gives business a family of compatible machines, and minicomputers bring a computer within reach of a single department.

checkpoints.name: Fourth generation: microprocessors
checkpoints.note: From 1971 a whole processor fits on one chip, and the computer becomes personal: on the desk, then on the lap, then in the pocket. Textbooks differ on where this generation ends; many say it has not.

checkpoints.name: Fifth generation: AI and parallel machines
checkpoints.note: Computers built to learn and reason, using many processors at once. Japan set out to build them in 1982 and fell short. There is no agreed start date: textbooks say "the present and beyond", so the line drawn here at 2010 is only a guide.
